transcript: I didn't know much about this new play Punch by James Graham before seeing it on Broadway, but it ended up being right up my alley. I love docudrama and while this is not a verbatim piece, it tells the true story of Jacob Dunne and the accidentally fatal punch that he threw at James Hodgkinson in 2011. And then, through a restorative justice program, he ended up coming in contact with James's parents and eventually meeting them. This is a tough watch, and despite its fast moving Act 1, I'd really describe this as a slow burn emotionally, culminating in an extremely hard-hitting scene in Act 2. I thought this production was great, from the pacing to the somewhat brutalist and urban set design, the lyrical staging, and Will Harrison's incredible leading performance as Jacob. I also noticed that this production incorporates a lot of movement and a pulsing underscore that makes the spare moments of stillness and silence especially impactful. That sense of balance and contrast is evident throughout the entire piece and is what makes it so thought provoking. Even just the choice of having Jacob as the narrator who tells the story in the first person forces us to humanize him before any redemption is evident. The way the story progresses is interesting, but it's not like there are big plot twists or anything — it's more of a window into experiences and facets of humanity that are seldom staged. This play has giving me a lot to chew on, as has the post-performance talkback we got to witness with some folks behind the play and the real story. Punch is currently running at MTC's Samuel J Friedman Theatre and it is really worth seeing. With that, another Playbill for my collection.

The only slight reservations are that it's a 'tough watch' and a 'slow burn,' but these are presented as positives rather than negatives.
